facts.fact: Adult fish need about 3% of their body weight in food per day for maintenance; fry and fingerlings can take up to 5%.
Most aquarium fish should be fed at least once a day; carnivores that take large meals may need only one or two feedings a week.
Most fish do well on one feeding a day or two smaller meals.
Fry and slow grazers may need 3 to 5 tiny meals a day, or a slow-breaking food such as gel food.
Large predatory fish may need only a few meals a week, while nano fish and fry eat more often.
Poor nutrition can cause poor growth, deformities, a weakened immune system, fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis) and impaired metabolism.
Feed about 10 to 15 minutes after the aquarium lights come on.
Feed nocturnal fish such as kuhli loaches and plecos after the lights go off.
Judge the portion by looking at the belly from the top and the side: aim for a slightly rounded abdomen.
Remove uneaten food after about 10 minutes.
Hikari advises offering only what fish eat in 3–5 minutes and removing uneaten food promptly.
Match the food to the fish's diet (carnivore, herbivore or omnivore), its mouth size, and whether it feeds at the surface, in midwater or on the bottom.
Surface feeders need floating food; bottom dwellers need food that sinks quickly.
Flakes can be too large for small-mouthed fish and can be crushed for them.
Mix live foods with commercial feeds to give variety and keep fish from refusing everything but one food.
Food forms include flakes, pellets, wafers, frozen, freeze-dried, gel and live foods.
Pellets come in various sizes and either float or sink; flakes weigh much less than pellets, so the same weight is a much larger volume.
Bettas need high-protein food and prefer floating food because their mouths point upward.
Goldfish are omnivores.
Signs of overfeeding: swollen belly, a lot of waste, little interest at mealtime, and uneaten food piling up, sometimes growing fungus.
An algae bloom or a boom in snails or worms can signal overfeeding.
Cloudy water, foam on the surface or high ammonia, nitrite or nitrate can signal overfeeding.
Signs of underfeeding are a thin body, a sunken belly and paler colours; fish that eat but stay thin may have internal parasites.
Overfeeding because fish beg: they often act hungry right after a meal.
Letting other household members feed the fish without the owner knowing, which leads to double feeding.
Forgetting nocturnal species that only feed after the lights go off.
The 'eat it in 5 minutes' rule is unreliable because feeding speed differs between species and between individual fish.
Feeding flakes to large fish such as oscars leaves uneaten flakes that foul the tank.
An occasional fasting day helps prevent problems from overfeeding.
Fatty liver is common in captive fish and can result from starvation, a diet high in carbohydrates or fats, or rancid feed.
Fish need vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in their diet, so most feeds should contain a stabilized form; a deficiency can cause 'broken back' disease with severe scoliosis.
Store dry feed in a pest-proof container in a cool, dry place: heat and humidity speed up spoilage, mould, possible mycotoxins and rancidity.
Throw away an opened container of feed kept at room temperature after 2 months.
Throw away commercial feeds stored in the freezer after 6 months, and commercial frozen foods (brine shrimp, bloodworms, mysids, glassworms) after 1 year.
Do not refreeze thawed feed.
Adult fish can often go about one week without food, depending on size, metabolism and water temperature; fry need an automatic feeder or a pet sitter.
Hikari says fish are most active at 68–78°F (20–26°C), when 2–4 small meals a day can be given; above 82°F (28°C) their metabolism slows.
In water above 82°F (28°C), Hikari recommends easily digested wheat-germ-based food in small portions, without going over the daily total (advice aimed at pond koi and goldfish).
Warm water holds less oxygen, which stresses fish; more aeration, plants or shade help.
Heat and humidity speed the spoilage of dry fish food, which matters in a hot, humid climate.
Vietnamese shops call commercial dry food 'cám công nghiệp' (or 'cám cá').

Vietnamese names for betta foods: sâu máu / ấu trùng muỗi (bloodworms), ấu trùng tôm nước mặn / Artemia (brine shrimp), trùn chỉ (tubifex), giun mẻ (microworms), thức ăn đông lạnh (frozen food), thức ăn viên (pellets).

A Vietnamese flowerhorn keeper reports feeding wild small fish (lia thia, cá trâm), live shrimp (tép), feeder carp, cá ròng ròng, trùn chỉ, mosquito larvae (lăng quăng), frozen beef heart, basa fillet and homemade blends.
The same keeper names feeder carp as the main way white spot (Ichthyophthirius) gets into the tank, and links densely raised ròng ròng fry to gut infections.
The same keeper reports that tubifex are often contaminated because they live in polluted water, and holds them under strong aeration for about a day, or freezes them, before feeding.
The same keeper quarantines feeder carp in salted water for several days, and freezes snails for a while to kill parasites before feeding them.
The same keeper changes water more often when feeding blended homemade food, because leftovers foul the tank.

A Vietnamese keeper reports that white maggots of the banana-stalk fly (ruồi cuống chuối, Telostylinus lineolatus) appeared on their own in a jar of infusoria culture (trùng cỏ), and that the fish ate them eagerly.
